catalog_quote: 1. Watam. This language is spoken on the eastern side of the mouth of the Sepik River. As I was unable to meet these people, I give here a brief analysis of notes published by R. Pöch in his article "Reisen an die Nord-Küste von Kaiser Wilhelmsland," in Globus, Band XCII, No. 18. His vocabulary has been added to the general vocabulary at the end of this article, so far as the two overlap, but no check on the accuracy of his phonetics is possible. For this reason I do not attempt to give a table of sounds. There is no sign in the word-list of noun class, or any special set of endings which mark nouns, as in Makarub and Murusapa. Syllables may be closed and a considerable variety of consonants appear as finals. Stress as marked by Pöch is also variable, but a tendency to final stress may be observed. This is not uncommon in this region.
world_status: statement found in an open source

This is not uncommon in this region.' Read the whole Watam section (pp. 132-133): Capell adds nothing further on stress, but his own re…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress tends to fall on the final syllable of the word, but is variable (not fully regular), as read off the acute accents in Pöch's 1904 Watam word list; Pöch's own marks (Globus 93, 1908, pp. 172-173, held by the project) put the accent on the last syllable in most words (gakú, oróp, arúm, kapúr, namót, pangán, endó, warkám, nakái, birák) with a minority non-final (girámo, poúrek, bámbam, apúpu).
new_statements.exceptions: Capell: stress 'is also variable'; only a 'tendency' to final stress. Pöch's list has several non-final accents (girámo 'three', poúrek 'four', bámbam 'sea fish sp.', apúpu 'shell axe', joberbe 'drum' unmarked).
new_statements.domain_note: Citation forms in an ethnographer's word list (Pöch, Watam village, 1904), analysed by Capell without hearing the language; no phrase-level information. Capell explicitly declines to give a table of sounds because Pöch's phonetics cannot be checked.
new_statements.identity_note: Language-level glottocode wata1253 (Watam; Ethnologue/SIL name Marangis). Pöch's 1904 word list and Foley's fieldwork are from Watam village at the Sepik mouth; Z'graggen 1971 notes Marangis village adopted the Watam language. No dialect distinctions are drawn in any source seen. Kopar (kopa1240) is a separate Lower Sepik language, not Watam, despite Haberland's 1966 listing.

sources.citation: Levy, Catherine. 2002. A tentative phonology and morphology of Awar, Lower Ramu family, Madang Province, PNG. PhD, Université Libre de Bruxelles.
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: Sister language only. p. 2: 'William Foley has written an unpublished grammar of Watam (1992), to which the author has had access through personal communications.' Awar sec. 4 'Stress pattern' (p. 82): 'In the word, the stress usually falls on the last syllable, for simple and compound words'. Nothing about Watam stress.

sources.citation: Foley, William A. c.1997. 'Watam' and 'Watam cont.' (research pages, Dept of Linguistics, University of Sydney; dated 29 July 1997). Internet Archive copy 2002-11-02 and 2001-02-24.
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: 'Watam Phonology' paragraph: 19 consonants and 5 vowels /i e a o u/, no fricatives, four places of articulation, four stop series (oral voiceless, oral voiced, nasal, prenasalized), glides /y w/ and tap /r/, loss of central vowels. Nothing on stress, accent, tone or syllable structure; remaining sections are word classes, nouns, verbs, word order/focus, serialization, discourse.

sources.citation: Z'graggen, John A. 1971. Classificatory and typological studies in languages of the Madang District. Pacific Linguistics C-19. Sec. 2.23.11.11 'Watam' (language 47/Wt).
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: Nothing on Watam stress; general note p. 6 that stress marking is omitted because the patterning is not established. Watam section: 'The first record of the Watam language was given by Pöch (1908: 170ff). Capell (1952: 132ff) incorporated this material.. Since then, no further fieldwork has been carried out'; his own data from Marangis village, whose people 'have adopted the Watam language'.
